“It can cause significant postpartum haemorrhage and may also lead to infection. If the placenta is abnormally adherent, attempts at removal can result in catastrophic haemorrhage.”

“I would assess the mother and baby immediately after birth and ensure appropriate neonatal care. I would manage the third stage actively where appropriate, including administration of a prophylactic uterotonic according to local protocol. I would assess for signs of placental separation and, when appropriate, perform controlled cord traction with suprapubic countertraction. Once the placenta is delivered, I would inspect it and the membranes for completeness, assess uterine tone and blood loss, and examine the vagina and perineum for trauma. I would continue monitoring the mother's vital signs and bleeding and escalate immediately if postpartum haemorrhage occurs.”

blocks.text: “I would suspect uterine atony, call for help if bleeding is significant, perform uterine massage, assess and quantify blood loss, administer appropriate uterotonics and simultaneously look for other causes of haemorrhage such as retained tissue or genital tract trauma.”

blocks.text: “I would assess the duration of the third stage, maternal condition and blood loss. I would avoid excessive cord traction, call for senior assistance, and if the placenta remains undelivered beyond the relevant threshold or there is significant bleeding, arrange appropriate intervention, including manual removal under suitable analgesia/anaesthesia when indicated.”
“What if there is heavy bleeding but the placenta has not delivered?”

“I would treat this as an obstetric emergency. I would call for senior help, begin ABC resuscitation, obtain large-bore IV access, send blood tests and crossmatch, assess uterine tone and the genital tract, administer appropriate uterotonics where indicated and arrange urgent management of the retained placenta, including theatre/manual removal when appropriate.”

“How do you manage the third stage of labour?”

blocks.text: “The third stage begins after delivery of the baby and ends with delivery of the placenta and membranes. I would assess both mother and baby immediately after birth and use active management where appropriate. I would administer a prophylactic uterotonic according to local protocol, monitor maternal observations and uterine tone, and look for signs of placental separation. Once separation has occurred, I would perform controlled cord traction with suprapubic countertraction by a trained practitioner. After delivery, I would inspect the placenta and membranes for completeness, assess uterine tone and blood loss, and examine the genital tract for trauma. If the placenta is retained, there is excessive bleeding, uterine atony or suspected uterine inversion, I would call for senior help immediately and manage the complication appropriately.”
